item.title: Answering in under a breath: voice AI agents for a Mexican e-commerce marketplace
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: How a Mexican marketplace can run Spanish voice AI agents for order calls on an open framework, with latency budgets, human handover and data rights built in
item.content:encoded:
A Mexican marketplace took most of its customer calls about one thing: where is my order. Wait times grew every sales season. Voice AI agents could answer those calls, but only if they sounded natural in Mexican Spanish, responded fast enough to feel like a conversation, handed over to people gracefully and respected callers' data rights. The architecture had to make all four true at once.

The situation

A marketplace in Mexico sold electronics, home goods and fashion from thousands of sellers, with deliveries handled by several carriers. Its contact centre took calls in Spanish, and most of them were about the same few things: where an order was, when it would arrive, how to change the address, how to start a return. During sales seasons, queues grew long enough that callers hung up and tried again, which made the queues longer.

Why now. On 29 October 2026, Deepgram announced it is acquiring Daily, the company behind Pipecat, a widely used open-source framework for real-time voice agents1. Both companies said Pipecat will stay under its BSD licence and move to an independent foundation whose steering committee includes Deepgram's competitors2. For a team choosing a voice agent stack, that settled the main worry about building on an open framework. On the legal side, Mexico's new personal data protection law took effect in March 202534, and legal commentary notes a right to object to automated processing that significantly affects people without human involvement3. Callers would always need a route to a person.

What had to be true

  • Natural Mexican Spanish, including regional accents, background noise and code-switching with English product names.
  • Conversational speed: replies quick enough that silence never feels like a dropped call.
  • Grounded answers only: order status from the systems, never from the model's imagination.
  • A person on request, with the conversation so far passed across.
  • Clear data rules for recordings and transcripts, and no lock-in to one speech vendor.

Architecture

The data flow, end to end

The hard part: latency you can feel

In text chat, a two-second delay is fine. On a phone call it feels like the line has dropped. The delay a caller hears is the sum of several stages: detecting that they stopped speaking, finishing speech recognition, the model's first tokens, any tool calls, and the first audio from speech synthesis. Each stage looked acceptable alone; together they were too slow.

The team set a latency budget per stage and traced every call end to end, so each turn showed exactly where the time went, in the same way distributed tracing shows which service in a request is slow5. That made the fixes obvious: stream everything instead of waiting for whole sentences; prefetch the caller's recent orders as soon as they are verified, so the first tool call is usually instant; use a smaller, faster model for routine turns; and play a short natural acknowledgement while a slow carrier API responds.

Turn-taking was the other half. Callers interrupt, pause mid-sentence and talk over the agent. The framework's interruption handling let the agent stop speaking when the caller started, and tuning silence detection for Spanish speech patterns cut the most awkward moments. See model routing and prompt caching for latency.

Voice agents are judged in hundreds of milliseconds. Budget latency per stage, trace every turn, and stream everything that can be streamed.

How it ran

Key decisions and trade-offs

DecisionAlternativeWhy
Open-source frameworkA closed voice agent platformSwap speech and model providers; no lock-in
Stream every stageSentence-by-sentence processingThe only way to stay inside the latency budget
Narrow tools for order dataGive the model raw order recordsGrounded answers and less personal data exposed
Disclose AI and offer a person upfrontOnly hand over on failureTrust, and respects the right to object
Off-peak rollout firstLaunch for a sales seasonLearn under low risk before peak load

What I'd do again, and differently

Again: build the evaluation set from real call recordings before choosing providers. Speech models that tested well on clean audio struggled with real calls. Differently: trace latency per stage from the first prototype, not after the first complaints. Related: evaluating AI agents, an agent-ready travel marketplace, today's tech news and where I work.

item.title: From guidelines to plumbing: putting MAS's AI risk management guidelines to work at a Singapore wealth manager
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: How a Singapore wealth manager can put MAS's final AI risk management guidelines into practice: an AI inventory, risk tiers, vendor assessments and lifecycle evidence.
item.content:encoded:
A Singapore wealth manager had AI everywhere and an inventory nowhere: vendor copilots, a suitability model, generative AI drafting client letters, and agents piloted by operations. MAS's final guidelines on AI risk management made the board accountable for all of it. The task was to turn the guidelines into systems that keep the inventory, the controls and the evidence current without a spreadsheet army.

The situation

A Singapore-based wealth manager served private and affluent clients across Asia. AI had arrived from every direction: a suitability scoring model built in-house, a vendor's generative AI assistant for relationship managers, a document tool that drafted client letters, transaction monitoring with machine learning inside, and an operations pilot using AI agents to reconcile statements. Risk kept a short spreadsheet of "AI models". Nobody believed it was complete.

Why now. The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) issued its final Guidelines on Artificial Intelligence Risk Management on 7 October 202613. Published summaries describe guidelines that cover all forms of AI, including generative AI and agents, on a risk-proportionate basis; that put boards and senior management in charge of AI risk appetite and oversight; and that keep the institution accountable for AI bought from vendors23. Commentary reports transition periods into 2027 and 20283. The authoritative text sits with MAS4. The board wanted to know what the firm actually used, how risky each use was, and how it would know when something went wrong.

What had to be true

  • A complete, living inventory of AI, built and bought, including features inside vendor products.
  • Risk tiers that change the controls: light for low-risk uses, rigorous for client-impacting ones.
  • Vendor AI held to the same bar, with evidence proportionate to risk.
  • Gates in the lifecycle: material AI cannot go live without evaluations and monitoring.
  • Board reporting from live data, not quarterly heroics.

Architecture

The data flow, end to end

The hard part: finding the AI you did not build

Most of the firm's AI was inside products it had bought. Vendors had switched on generative features in CRM, document and communications tools, often by default. Interviews missed them. The team used three nets: every generative AI call from internal systems went through an LLM gateway, which logged the application and model; procurement and renewals now asked vendors to declare AI features and their data use; and a periodic scan looked for AI SDKs and API keys in code and configuration. Each find created a draft inventory entry for an owner to complete.

Monitoring had a consistency problem. Each tool reported AI activity differently, so dashboards were stitched together by hand. The team adopted the OpenTelemetry generative AI conventions as the firm's telemetry contract and checked conformance in CI, so a service that emitted the wrong attributes failed its build rather than quietly breaking reports. OpenTelemetry Weaver provides exactly that kind of live check against a registry of conventions5.

Agents needed their own treatment. The reconciliation pilot was low risk in impact but high in autonomy, so its tier was raised: every action logged, narrow permissions and a human approval step for anything that changed client records. See when agents become the user and evaluating AI agents.

An AI inventory kept by survey is out of date the day it is finished. Wire discovery into the gateway, procurement and the codebase, and let people complete what the systems find.

How it ran

Key decisions and trade-offs

DecisionAlternativeWhy
Discover through systemsAnnual surveysInventory stays current as tools change
Tier by impact, autonomy and dataOne control set for all AIProportionate effort, as the guidelines intend
All generative AI through one gatewayDirect calls from each appVisibility, policy and cost in one place
Telemetry contract checked in CIDashboards fixed by handReliable evidence without manual effort
Evidence from vendors by tierAccept self-attestation everywhereAccountability stays with the firm

What I'd do again, and differently

Again: put the gateway in early. It quickly found AI uses the survey had missed. Differently: involve procurement from the start. Vendor features switched on at renewal were the largest source of new entries. Related: ISO 42001 and the NIST AI RMF, LLM observability with OpenTelemetry, an agent-ready marketplace in Southeast Asia and the Singapore page.

item.title: Our models, our metal: a sovereign LLM platform for a European telecom operator
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: How a European telecom operator can run open-weight LLMs on its own GPUs for network, care and security teams, with NIS2-grade controls and a hosted fallback.
item.content:encoded:
A telecom operator in central Europe wanted generative AI for network operations, customer care and security, but would not send network configurations, customer records or incident data to an outside model. Capable open-weight models made running its own platform realistic. The task was to build one that is shared, secure, reliable and honest about cost.

The situation

A telecom operator in central Europe ran fixed and mobile networks for several million customers. Three teams wanted generative AI: network operations, to read alarms and configuration changes; customer care, to summarise interactions and draft replies; and security, to triage alerts and investigate incidents. Each had started its own pilot with a different hosted model, and the security and legal teams had stopped all three because network topology, customer data and incident details were leaving the company.

Why now. Telecom operators are essential entities under the EU's NIS2 Directive, with duties covering risk management, supply-chain security and incident reporting4. Transposition has been uneven, and the Commission took several member states to the Court of Justice in July 2026 for not implementing it3, but national laws are now arriving; Austria's, for example, applies from 1 October 20262. At the same time, capable open-weight models became realistic to run in-house; on 29 October 2026 Mistral released the weights of its trillion-parameter Large 4, pitched at security teams who want to run it on their own infrastructure1. The operator decided to build one shared, sovereign platform rather than three pilots.

What had to be true

  • Sensitive data stays in-house: network, customer and incident data only touch the operator's own infrastructure.
  • One platform, three tenants, with quotas, policies and costs kept separate.
  • Models chosen by evidence: evaluations on each team's real tasks.
  • Reliable on imperfect hardware: GPU, driver and node failures must not take services down.
  • A sensible escape hatch: hosted models for non-sensitive work, through the same controls.

Architecture

The data flow, end to end

The hard part: running GPUs like a utility

Buying GPUs was the easy part. Keeping them useful was not. Multi-GPU model servers are sensitive to hardware faults, driver updates and slow terminations, and Kubernetes' traditional view of devices as either present or absent does not cope well with partial failures. The Kubernetes community has documented these failure modes, from device plugin restarts to pods holding devices while they shut down5.

The team designed for those failures: health checks on GPUs and model servers, spare capacity so a failed node does not halve a model pool, staged driver and plugin updates, and a gateway that retries on a healthy replica. Scheduling moved to Dynamic Resource Allocation so model servers could ask for the exact accelerators they needed; see DRA for GPU scheduling. Sharing used quotas per tenant, with security given priority during incidents.

Model choice was the other discipline. The largest open models are impressive and expensive to hold in memory. Each tenant built an evaluation set from real tasks, and the gateway routed each task to the smallest model that met its quality bar, keeping the largest model for hard security investigations. More in running a trillion-parameter model yourself and the AI memory squeeze.

Self-hosting is an operations commitment, not a download. Budget for spare capacity, failure handling and evaluation before you budget for the biggest model.

How it ran

Key decisions and trade-offs

DecisionAlternativeWhy
One shared platformA cluster per teamScarce GPUs used well; one set of controls
Gateway enforces data classificationTrust each applicationOne place to prove where data went
Smallest model that passes evaluationLargest model everywhereLower memory, cost and latency
Spare capacity for failuresRun GPUs at full allocationService survives node and driver failures
Hosted fallback for non-sensitive tasksIn-house onlyHandles peaks without overbuying hardware

What I'd do again, and differently

Again: put the gateway in first. It stopped the data leaks on day one and let the platform change underneath without tenant rework. Differently: run failure drills before the first production tenant, not after the first outage. Related: Kubernetes inference gateway, serving with vLLM, telecom observability and SLOs and the Europe page.

item.title: Results, records and research: a consent-aware data platform for an Indian diagnostics chain
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: How an Indian diagnostics chain can share lab results through ABDM, build research-ready data and meet the DPDP Rules' November 2026 and May 2027 milestones.
item.content:encoded:
A diagnostics chain ran hundreds of collection centres and several regional labs. Patients wanted results in their digital health records, doctors wanted trends, and the business wanted to use its data for research and AI. India's data protection rules arrive in phases through 2027. The platform had to make every use of a patient's data traceable to a purpose and, where needed, to consent.

The situation

A diagnostics chain in India ran collection centres, home sample collection and several regional laboratories. Results went out as PDFs by email and WhatsApp. Each lab used its own test codes, so a haemoglobin result from one city did not match the same test from another. The analytics team copied production tables into a warehouse with names and phone numbers intact, and the business wanted to start using the data for research partnerships and AI models.

Why now. India's Digital Personal Data Protection Rules were notified in November 2025 and apply in phases1. The consent manager framework applies from 13 November 2026, and most obligations on data fiduciaries, including notices, consent, data principal rights, breach reporting and children's data, from 13 May 202723. At the same time, the Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission (ABDM) gives patients a digital health account and a consent-based way to share records between providers4. The chain wanted to join that ecosystem properly and be ready for the DPDP deadlines in one programme.

What had to be true

  • Purpose for every use: reporting results, billing, analytics, research and AI, each with a recorded basis.
  • Patient-approved sharing of results into digital health records through ABDM.
  • One meaning per test: local codes mapped to a standard terminology once.
  • Research kept apart: pseudonymised, purpose-bound and never mixed with operations.
  • Breach-ready: detection, assessment and reporting routes tested before May 2027.

Architecture

The data flow, end to end

The hard part: one test, many meanings, many purposes

The first problem was meaning. Each lab had grown its own test catalogue, so the same test had different codes and units across cities. Mapping every local code to LOINC once, with the mapping owned by a clinical team and versioned, made results comparable for doctors and usable for research. See clinical terminologies and OMOP vocabularies.

The second was purpose. Operational use, such as reporting a result, rests on a different basis from research. The team kept them physically apart. The research store follows the OMOP Common Data Model, built through a planned extract, transform and load process that starts with the person and visit structure before clinical tables5, and it only ever receives pseudonymised data for recorded purposes. See FHIR to OMOP architecture.

The third was withdrawal. A patient who withdraws consent for research must be removed from future extracts, and the system must be able to show that. Because every research load is driven by the consent service, a withdrawal stops the next load and is recorded against the patient's consent history.

Consent is not a checkbox at registration. It is a record that every pipeline reads before it moves data.

How it ran

Key decisions and trade-offs

DecisionAlternativeWhy
Central consent and purpose serviceConsent flags in each systemOne record every pipeline checks
Map to LOINC onceMap per use caseConsistent meaning for care and research
Separate pseudonymised research storeResearch on the warehousePurposes stay separate and auditable
Design for consent managers nowWait for registrationsInterfaces ready when managers arrive
Remove identified warehouse copiesRestrict access onlyData that is not there cannot leak

What I'd do again, and differently

Again: put clinicians in charge of terminology mapping. It was the foundation for everything else. Differently: deal with the identified warehouse copies on day one. They were the largest risk and the easiest to remove. Related: a DPDP-ready consent platform for lending, a FHIR and OMOP evidence platform, India's proposed frontier AI law and the India page.

item.title: Ready for 10 December: automated decision transparency for an Australian energy retailer
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: How an Australian energy retailer can meet the Privacy Act's automated decision disclosure duty from 10 December 2026: find every decision, record it and explain it.
item.content:encoded:
An energy retailer used software to run credit checks, set payment plans, flag hardship and trigger collections, across systems built over twenty years. From 10 December 2026, Australian organisations must explain in their privacy policy when computer programs make or substantially inform decisions that significantly affect people. The retailer first had to find out where that happened.

The situation

An Australian energy retailer served households and small businesses across several states. Software touched many decisions that matter to customers: credit checks at sign-up, security deposits, payment plan offers, hardship flags, collections steps and, at the end of the line, disconnection warnings. The logic lived in a billing platform from the 2000s, a CRM, a collections tool, a credit bureau integration and a newer machine learning model that predicted who might struggle to pay.

Why now. From 10 December 2026, APP entities must include information in their privacy policy when they have arranged for a computer program to make, or do something substantially and directly related to making, decisions that significantly affect individuals' rights or interests1. The OAIC published its final guidance on 30 September 20264. Commentary on that guidance reads it broadly: it reaches rules engines and decision-support tools, not only AI, and human review does not automatically take a decision out of scope23. The retailer's privacy policy said nothing about any of this, and nobody could list where it applied.

What had to be true

  • A complete list of significant decisions that software makes or substantially informs.
  • Disclosures that match reality, generated from that list and kept current.
  • Evidence for each decision: which system, which logic version, which data.
  • Explanations on request that customer service can give in plain language.
  • No new hidden decisions: changes to decision logic registered before release.

Architecture

The data flow, end to end

The hard part: finding decisions in twenty-year-old systems

Nobody had a list. Decision logic sat in billing configuration tables, stored procedures, collections scripts and a model in a notebook pipeline. Interviews found the obvious decisions; data found the rest. The team traced customer journeys that ended in a significant outcome, such as a deposit request or a disconnection warning, back through the systems that produced them, and recorded every step where software chose or ranked something.

Capturing evidence without rewriting the billing platform was the second problem. The OpenTelemetry Collector can read existing log files and query databases through receivers, then forward everything in one format, which is how the OpenTelemetry community recommends bringing older systems into modern observability5. The team used it to turn existing logs and table changes into structured decision events, with no change to the legacy code.

The scope calls were made with counsel. Following the guidance's broad reading, the team treated borderline cases as in scope, including the payment difficulty model, even though a person made the final hardship decision23. The hardship model was also a reason for care: it informed help for vulnerable customers, so its explanations were written with the hardship team. See explainable credit decisions in Brazil for the reason-code pattern.

You cannot disclose what you have not found. The privacy policy paragraph is the last step; the inventory is the work.

How it ran

Key decisions and trade-offs

DecisionAlternativeWhy
Treat borderline cases as in scopeNarrow reading to limit disclosureMatches the guidance and avoids later corrections
Generate disclosures from the registerWrite the policy section by handPolicy stays true as systems change
Capture events from logs and databasesModify legacy codeFaster, lower risk before the deadline
Release gate on decision logicPeriodic audits onlyNew decisions cannot appear unnoticed
Write explanations with hardship staffEngineering-written reasonsClear and appropriate for vulnerable customers

What I'd do again, and differently

Again: trace from outcomes backwards. It found decisions no interview would have surfaced, such as a deposit rule hidden in a billing configuration table. Differently: start the release gate first. Two new rules went live during the inventory and had to be found again. Related: policy layers for AI assistants, ISO 42001 and the NIST AI RMF, AI provider resilience under CPS 230 and the Australia page.

item.title: Faster repairs, fair decisions: AI agents for a UK housing association under the new automated decision rules
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: How a UK housing association can use AI agents to triage repairs and spot vulnerable tenants under the DUAA's automated decision rules and Awaab's Law timescales.
item.content:encoded:
A housing association received thousands of repair requests a month by phone, web and email, and missed hazards hidden in the backlog. Damp and mould now carry legal deadlines, and the UK's rules on automated decisions have changed. The aim was to use AI agents to read, classify and route every request quickly, while keeping people in charge of decisions that affect tenants.

The situation

A housing association in England managed tens of thousands of homes. Repair requests arrived by phone, web form, email and through housing officers, and were keyed into the housing management system by a contact centre. At busy times, requests waited days to be read. A message mentioning "black marks on the bedroom wall" or "the baby keeps coughing" could sit in the same queue as a dripping tap.

Why now. Two sets of rules changed the stakes. Awaab's Law requires social landlords to investigate and fix damp, mould and serious hazards within set timescales, with the first phase in force since October 20255. And the Data (Use and Access) Act replaced the UK GDPR's rules on automated decisions with new Articles 22A to 22D from 5 February 2026, permitting more automated decision-making but with safeguards such as information, the right to contest and human intervention23. The ICO has said it is working on updated guidance and a code of practice on AI and automated decisions1, and in October 2026 it set out its expectations for AI agents and called for views4. The association needed speed and safeguards together.

What had to be true

  • Every request read on arrival, whatever the channel.
  • Hazards escalated by rules, with statutory clocks that start when the landlord becomes aware.
  • People decide what significantly affects tenants; AI classifies, summarises and suggests.
  • Every step traceable, so complaints and the Housing Ombudsman can see what happened and why.
  • Tenants can challenge an outcome and reach a person.

Architecture

The data flow, end to end

The hard part: long-running cases that must not get lost

A repair case is not a single model call. It can run for weeks: classify, wait for a surveyor, wait for a tenant to confirm access, raise a job, wait for a contractor, check it is fixed. Agents built as simple request-and-response loops lose state when a service restarts, and nobody notices until a statutory deadline has passed.

The team ran each case as a durable workflow. The workflow engine records every step, so a case resumes exactly where it was after a failure, and it can wait days for a person or a contractor without holding resources. Tracing had to follow the whole case, not just individual calls; the OpenTelemetry and Dapr communities have worked on carrying trace context across the workflow engine's internal boundaries so steps form one coherent trace6.

The second hard part was deciding where automation stops. Classification and routing of ordinary repairs were automated end to end. Anything that could significantly affect a tenant, such as refusing a repair, deciding it was the tenant's responsibility or flagging possible vulnerability, went to a person with the agent's summary and evidence. That kept the association comfortably within the safeguards the new rules expect, and made challenges easy to handle3. See structured outputs for how the classifications were kept reliable.

Automate the reading, the routing and the reminders. Keep people on the decisions a tenant might want to argue with.

How it ran

Key decisions and trade-offs

DecisionAlternativeWhy
Rules own statutory prioritiesLet the model rank urgencyDeadlines must be predictable and auditable
People decide significant outcomesFully automated decisions with safeguardsLower risk and easier challenges
Durable workflowsAgent loops with a databaseCases survive failures and long waits
Structured outputsFree-text summariesReliable routing and measurable accuracy
Shadow mode before routingSwitch on and monitorFind misses without risk to tenants

What I'd do again, and differently

Again: let housing staff define hazards and vulnerability in their own words, then turn those into rules and test cases. Differently: bring the complaints team in from the start. Their cases were the best test set we had. Related: evaluating AI agents, agents as users of enterprise systems, UK cyber resilience readiness and the UK page.

item.title: Ready before it bites: AI data governance for a Japanese retail chain under the amended APPI
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: How a Japanese retail chain can prepare its AI and camera analytics for the amended APPI: purpose-tagged data, facial data controls, contractor limits and evidence.
item.content:encoded:
A Japanese retail chain used loyalty data to forecast demand and store cameras to understand footfall, with several contractors doing the analytics. Japan's amended privacy law is now on the books, adding surcharges, rules for facial data and a route for using personal data in statistics and AI development. The duties are not in force yet. The aim was to make the data estate ready before they are.

The situation

A Japanese retail chain with several hundred stores ran a loyalty programme, an app and in-store cameras. Its data team trained demand forecasting and promotion models on loyalty purchases, and two outside contractors analysed camera footage to measure footfall and queue times. The data had grown up over a decade: copies in the warehouse, the contractors' environments and a few notebooks, with no single record of where personal data went or why.

Why now. Japan's amended Act on the Protection of Personal Information was promulgated in July 2026 as Act No. 56 of 2026, with most duties starting on dates set later by Cabinet Order2. As reported, it introduces an administrative surcharge, adds rules for facial recognition data, makes contractors' duty not to use data beyond their task explicit, and creates a consent exception for statistical processing and AI development13. Commentary expects strengthened penalties from early 2027 and the main reforms by mid-20282. The Personal Information Protection Commission (PPC) will set the detailed rules4. The chain wanted to use the time to get ready rather than react later.

What had to be true

  • Every dataset used for AI known: its source, purpose, legal basis and where copies live.
  • Facial data minimised: kept only where needed, disclosed clearly and never reused quietly.
  • Contractors bounded to the task they were hired for, technically and not just by contract.
  • Personal data out of telemetry by default.
  • Evidence on demand, ready to map to the PPC's rules when they arrive.

Architecture

The data flow, end to end

The hard part: cameras and contractors

The footfall project was the riskiest part of the estate. Contractors received video clips and ran their own models on them, which meant faces left the stores and their later use was hard to control. With facial data getting specific rules in the amendment1, the team changed the design rather than adding paperwork.

Video processing moved to on-premises devices in each store. They produce counts, dwell times and queue lengths, and discard frames after processing. Contractors now receive those aggregates, not footage. Where a use case truly needed identification, such as a loss-prevention pilot, it was split out as its own system with its own disclosure, retention and approval. That separation is what makes the purpose clear to customers and to a regulator.

Contractors moved into scoped workspaces on the chain's own platform, with access to named datasets for a set period, every query logged and no export by default. This turns the duty not to use data beyond the task into a technical control instead of a clause3.

The last gap was telemetry. Application logs and traces carried customer IDs, emails and auth headers, copied into tools that many people could see. The team set masking as the default in the OpenTelemetry pipeline, keeping useful context such as store or segment and hiding identifiers and credentials5.

The cheapest compliance is data you never collect. Change the design so the sensitive data does not leave the store, then govern what remains.

How it ran

Key decisions and trade-offs

DecisionAlternativeWhy
Process video at the edgeSend footage to contractorsFaces stay in the store; purpose is clear
Prepare nowWait for the PPC rulesInventory and redesign take longer than the rules will
Do not rely on the AI exception yetAssume all training is coveredIts reach depends on rules not yet issued
Contractor workspaces on our platformData shipped to contractor systemsTask limits enforced technically and logged
Mask telemetry by defaultClean up logs case by caseObservability tools are a common leak

What I'd do again, and differently

Again: redesign the camera use case instead of documenting it. It removed most of the risk in one move. Differently: put purpose tags on data at ingestion from the start, rather than adding them during the inventory; tagging old data took longer than building the platform. Related: ISO 42001 and the NIST AI RMF, high-impact AI under Korea's AI Basic Act and where I work.

item.title: Helpful, not reckless: privacy-first AI triage for a Kenyan telehealth service
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: How a Kenyan telehealth provider can use LLM triage in English and Swahili while meeting the Data Protection Act and the ODPC's draft AI guidance on health data.
item.content:encoded:
A Kenyan telehealth service wanted an AI assistant to take symptoms over chat, in English and Swahili, and route patients to the right clinician faster. Health data is the most sensitive data it holds, the best models run offshore, and Kenya's regulator is moving from warnings to enforcement. The design had to keep patients safe, keep identifiable data at home and prove both.

The situation

A telehealth provider in Kenya offered consultations by app, WhatsApp and SMS, backed by a network of clinicians and partner pharmacies. Demand peaked in the evenings, when patients waited longest for a first response. The team wanted an AI assistant to take a structured symptom history in English or Swahili, summarise it and suggest who should see the patient, so clinicians could start from a clear picture.

Why now. Kenya's Data Protection Act treats health data as sensitive personal data and allows transfers abroad only with appropriate safeguards1. The Office of the Data Protection Commissioner (ODPC) consulted in 2026 on draft guidance on AI2, and commentary on the draft says uses such as health diagnostics and clinical decision support would need a data protection impact assessment3. There were also public calls for stronger protection of data sent to offshore AI providers4, and an October 2026 report described African regulators, Kenya's among them, using data protection law to police AI while dedicated AI bills stall5. A dedicated AI law may or may not arrive soon. The data protection duties already apply.

What had to be true

  • Safety first: urgent symptoms escalated by rules, never left to a model's judgement.
  • Clinician in the loop: the AI drafts, a clinician decides.
  • Identifiable data stays home: names, numbers and IDs never reach an offshore model.
  • Both languages work, including mixed English and Swahili, tested on every change.
  • A living DPIA, updated with each release and backed by evidence.

Architecture

The data flow, end to end

The hard part: giving the model context without giving it identities

Good triage needs context: age band, past visits, current medicines, allergies. Shipping the whole record to the model would have been easy and wrong. The team instead exposed clinic systems through small MCP servers running in-country, each offering narrow, read-only tools such as "medicines for this patient token" or "visits in the last 90 days"6. The servers return only the fields the tool needs, keyed by token, so the model can reason about the patient without ever seeing who they are.

De-identification in free text is harder than in records. Patients type names, phone numbers, locations and the names of relatives, often mixing English and Swahili. The gateway combined pattern rules with a small local model for entity detection, tested on real, consented examples in both languages, and failed closed: if it was unsure, the message went to a human rather than to the model. More on securing tool servers in the MCP security checklist.

The question is not "can we send this to the model?" but "what is the least the model needs to be useful?" Build tools that answer exactly that.

How it ran

Key decisions and trade-offs

DecisionAlternativeWhy
Rules before the model for red flagsLet the model spot emergenciesPredictable, testable and explainable
De-identify in-countrySend records under a contractIdentifiable health data never leaves
Narrow MCP toolsGive the model the whole recordLeast data for each question
Fail closed on uncertain redactionSend and hopeA human is cheaper than a breach
Shadow mode before assistPilot directly with patientsFind errors without risk to care

What I'd do again, and differently

Again: shadow mode. It showed where the model asked poor follow-up questions in Swahili before any patient saw them. Differently: build the bilingual evaluation set first, not alongside the gateway. It was the slowest part to get right and it drove most design choices. Related: private AI for clinical documentation, private LLMs, evaluation sets, healthcare data architecture and where I work.

item.title: Onshore by January: moving Nigerian payment data home without breaking a pan-African platform
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: How a Lagos-based payments company can meet the CBN's 2027 payment data localisation deadline without splitting its platform: cells, data classes and tested cutover.
item.content:encoded:
A Lagos-based payments company ran one platform for Nigeria, Kenya and Ghana from an overseas cloud region. The Central Bank of Nigeria then set a deadline for payment transaction data generated in Nigeria to be stored in Nigeria. The task was to move that data onshore, keep one platform for every market and cut over without losing a payment.

The situation

A payments company headquartered in Lagos offered merchant collections, payouts and card processing in Nigeria, Kenya and Ghana. Nigeria was its largest market. Everything ran in one overseas public cloud region: one set of databases, one event stream, one analytics warehouse. It was simple to run, and every market shared the same release process.

Why now. The Central Bank of Nigeria directed banks, fintechs and other payment service providers to store payment transaction data generated in Nigeria on servers in Nigeria from 1 January 2027, with vendors that handle that data expected to align1. Legal commentary noted open questions, such as how "generated in Nigeria" applies to transactions that cross borders2. Separately, the federal government adopted a National Digital Cloud Policy in 2026, which commentators describe as classifying data and applying residency rules to defined sensitive and sovereign categories rather than all data34. With only months to the deadline, the company needed a plan it could execute, not a debate about interpretation.

What had to be true

  • Nigerian payment transaction data at rest and in processing in Nigeria by the deadline, including backups and logs.
  • One platform: the same code, pipelines and on-call for every market.
  • Every field classified, so engineers know what may leave a country and in what form.
  • No lost or duplicated payments during migration.
  • Vendors aligned: fraud, card and support tools that touch Nigerian payment data had to follow it.

Architecture

The data flow, end to end

The hard part: one platform, several homes

The tempting answer was to fork: copy the platform into a Nigerian data centre and run it separately. That doubles releases, on-call and drift. Instead, the team adopted a cell design. Each market runs as a cell with identical services, deployed from the same Git repository. The cells differ only in where they run and in the data rules applied to them.

Cluster API made that practical across very different infrastructure. A management cluster declares the workload clusters, whether they run in a Nigerian colocation facility or a public cloud region, and the same tooling creates, upgrades and replaces them5. The management cluster holds no payment data, so it can sit outside Nigeria.

The second hard part was the data no one thinks about: logs, traces, backups, support tickets and fraud vendor feeds. The team classified fields into a short list of classes, from public to payment transaction data, and enforced the classes in code: telemetry carried identifiers as tokens, backups were written to onshore storage only, and export pipelines refused unclassified fields. See data contracts for how to make that stick.

Localisation fails in the side channels. Classify logs, traces, backups and vendor feeds as carefully as the main database.

How it ran

Migration ran product by product, starting with payouts, which had the simplest flows. Databases were replicated into the Nigeria cell and both copies ran side by side, with reconciliation reports comparing every transaction, before traffic moved. Payment idempotency mattered here; see idempotent payment pipelines. After each cutover, overseas copies and backups were deleted on a recorded schedule.

Key decisions and trade-offs

DecisionAlternativeWhy
Cells on one codebaseFork a Nigerian platformOne release process and one on-call
Cluster API across colocation and cloudDifferent tooling per locationSame lifecycle everywhere
Tokens and aggregates cross bordersCopy full records to the group warehouseGroup reporting without moving payment data
Product-by-product cutoverOne big switchSmaller blast radius and real rollback
Classify telemetry and backupsFocus on primary databasesSide channels are where localisation breaks

What I'd do again, and differently

Again: classify before building. The classes answered most of the hard questions, including which vendors were affected. Differently: involve card and fraud vendors earlier. Their onshore options and timelines set the critical path more than our own engineering did. For related patterns, see a multi-cloud Terraform estate, Kubernetes multi-tenancy and where I work.

item.title: From voluntary to mandatory: an open finance platform for a mid-sized Colombian bank
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: How a mid-sized Colombian bank can prepare for mandatory open finance under Decree 368 of 2026: consent, secure APIs, data receiving and measurable reliability.
item.content:encoded:
Colombia has made open finance mandatory for supervised financial institutions. A mid-sized bank had to become both a reliable data provider and a capable data receiver, on standards still being written, without building twice. The answer was a platform designed around consent, security profiles and measurable service levels.

The situation

A mid-sized Colombian bank offered current accounts, cards and small business loans. It had taken part in the earlier, voluntary open finance scheme in a limited way: a few partner integrations, each built separately, with its own consent screens and its own security setup. Customer data lived in a core banking system, a card platform and a lending system, each with a different idea of what a "customer" was.

Why now. Decree 368 of 2026 made open finance mandatory for institutions supervised by the Financial Superintendence of Colombia (SFC), replacing the voluntary framework1. Supervised entities must act as both data providers and data receivers, and data can only flow with the customer's prior, express and informed consent2. The common technical standards are left to the SFC, and commentary on the decree sets out a deadline in October 2026 for the SFC to publish its schedule for them, with a period for institutions to comply after each standard is issued3. The bank had to start building before the details were final.

What had to be true

  • One consent model for every data flow, out and in, that customers can see and revoke.
  • Standards-ready APIs: a canonical internal model that can be mapped to the SFC standards as they arrive.
  • Financial-grade security for every third party, with no bespoke partner setups.
  • Measurable reliability: availability and latency per endpoint, because the regulator will publish indicators.
  • Useful received data: data from other institutions available to credit and product teams, with purpose recorded.

Architecture

The data flow, end to end

The hard part: building to standards that do not exist yet

The decree sets the framework, but the technical standards come later13. Waiting meant missing the window; building to a guess meant rework. The team separated what was certain from what was not.

Security was the most certain. Open finance schemes around the world converge on financial-grade API profiles, so the authorisation server was built to the OpenID Foundation's FAPI 2.0 Security Profile, with sender-constrained tokens and strong client authentication4. Whatever the local profile adds, most of that work carries over.

Data formats were the least certain. Instead of exposing internal systems directly, the team built a canonical model of customers, accounts, cards and loans, fed by change data capture from each source system. The public API shapes became a thin mapping layer on top. When the SFC publishes a standard, the change lands in the mapping, not in three core systems. More on that pattern in change data capture and event streams and data contracts.

Reliability had to be measurable from day one, because the SFC must publish indicators on the system2. The gateway emits a trace for every call, so availability and latency can be reported per endpoint and per participant, and a slow downstream system shows up in the trace rather than in a complaint5.

When the rules are still being written, build the parts every scheme shares, consent, security and measurement, and keep the parts that will change behind a thin mapping layer.

How it ran

Key decisions and trade-offs

DecisionAlternativeWhy
Build to FAPI 2.0 nowWait for the local profileSecurity work carries over; waiting costs months
Canonical model behind thin mappingsExpose source systems directlyStandards changes land in one place
Change data captureNightly batch extractsShared data must be current, and batch hides failures
One consent service for in and outSeparate provider and receiver consentOne place for customers to see and revoke
Trace every call at the gatewaySample or rely on logsRegulator indicators need complete, per-endpoint data

What I'd do again, and differently

Again: treat the receiver side as a product, not a compliance task. Data from other institutions is what makes open finance worth the cost, as the Brazilian lender found when it used consented data in credit decisions. Differently: start participant onboarding earlier. Technical integration was faster than agreeing testing and support arrangements with other institutions. Related: idempotent financial pipelines and where I work.

item.title: Guarding the keys: hardening the management plane of a US regional water and power utility
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: How a US regional water and power utility can protect the management tools attackers now target: isolated admin paths, strong identity, tamper-proof logs and drills.
item.content:encoded:
A regional utility had invested in protecting its control systems, but the tools that manage everything else, from firewalls and VPNs to endpoint and IT service platforms, sat on the ordinary corporate network. That is exactly where state-backed attackers have been looking. The goal was to make those management tools hard to reach, hard to abuse and impossible to use silently.

The situation

A regional utility in the United States supplied water and electricity to several counties. Its operational technology (OT) team had done solid work separating control systems from the corporate network. The IT side was different. Firewall and VPN consoles, an SD-WAN controller, the hypervisor manager, endpoint management, the IT service platform and the GIS server were all administered from ordinary laptops on the corporate network, several with web consoles reachable from the internet "for vendor support". Many admins had standing domain-wide rights.

Why now. In late October 2026, Lumen's Black Lotus Labs described Volt Typhoon's Silent Train framework: short-lived relay networks used in several zero-day campaigns against centralised management platforms, with victims including energy, water and transport organisations12. The same week, Help Net Security reported a China-nexus group using a VMware ESX logging flaw as a zero-day to hide its activity4. CISA and partners had already warned in 2024 that Volt Typhoon seeks persistent access to US critical infrastructure, living off the land and abusing valid accounts3. The utility's board asked a simple question: if someone took over our management tools, would we know?

What had to be true

  • No management interface on the internet, and every one inventoried with an owner.
  • Administration only from dedicated, hardened workstations on an isolated network.
  • No standing admin rights: access granted for a task, approved and time-limited.
  • Logs that survive a compromise: shipped off the device, to storage the attacker cannot edit.
  • A practised response for "a management tool is compromised", including OT impact.

Architecture

The data flow, end to end

The hard part: telemetry an attacker cannot erase

Attackers who reach a management tool tend to clean up after themselves, and the ESX case shows they will use logging weaknesses to hide4. Logs that stay on the device prove little. The team made off-device telemetry the rule: firewalls, VPN concentrators, hypervisors and consoles send logs to OpenTelemetry Collectors at each site, which forward them over mutually authenticated TLS to a central collector behind a gateway that terminates mTLS5. From there, data lands in write-once storage with its own separate admin path.

Two details mattered. First, the logging pipeline had its own credentials and admins, so taking over the firewall console did not also give control of the logs about it. Second, detections focused on behaviour CISA describes for this actor, such as valid accounts used at odd times, new admin accounts and configuration exports, rather than malware signatures3.

If the people who administer a system also administer its logs, you do not have evidence. You have a diary the attacker can edit.

How it ran

Key decisions and trade-offs

DecisionAlternativeWhy
Dedicated admin workstationsAdmin from everyday laptopsPhishing and browsing never touch admin sessions
Isolated admin networkFirewall rules on the corporate networkOne path to watch and defend
Just-in-time accessStanding domain admin rightsStolen accounts are useless most of the time
Separate admins for loggingSame team runs systems and logsEvidence survives a console takeover
Brokered vendor sessionsInternet-facing consoles for vendorsSupport without permanent exposure

What I'd do again, and differently

Again: start with the inventory. Several consoles nobody owned turned up, including two still facing the internet. Differently: involve the main vendors in week one. Their support processes, not our technology, were the slowest part to change. For the patching side, see defender-first AI models and vulnerability management, this week's tech news brief, securing a legacy PHP estate and OpenTelemetry in practice.

item.title: Decisions people can question: explainable AI credit scoring for a Brazilian digital lender
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: How a Brazilian digital lender can make AI credit decisions reviewable under the LGPD and ready for Brazil's AI bill: reason codes, human review and traceable decisions.
item.content:encoded:
A Brazilian digital lender approved and priced loans in seconds with machine learning models. Customers could not easily find out why they were declined, and reviewing a decision meant digging through logs. The goal was to make every automated credit decision explainable, reviewable by a person and ready for the AI rules Brazil is debating.

The situation

A digital lender in Brazil offered personal loans and credit lines through its app. Machine learning models approved, declined and priced applications in seconds, using bureau data, open finance data shared with consent and in-app behaviour. Growth was strong. Complaints were the warning sign: declined customers could not get a useful answer about why, and when the team reviewed a decision it meant piecing together logs from several services.

Why now. Brazil's data protection law, the LGPD, already gives people the right to request review of decisions taken solely through automated processing that affect their interests, including credit profiling, and to receive clear information about the criteria used1. The national data protection authority, ANPD, oversees it2. On top of that, Brazil's AI bill, PL 2338/2023, passed the Senate in December 2024 and was pending in the Chamber of Deputies, with a vote reported as expected after the October 2026 elections345. It is not law yet, but a lender relying on automated credit decisions could not afford to wait.

What had to be true

  • Every decision reconstructable: model version, data used and outcome, stored together.
  • Clear reasons a customer can understand, without exposing trade secrets.
  • Human review on request, handled quickly with full context.
  • Governed models: tested before release and monitored after.
  • Data minimised and documented, especially open finance data used with consent.

Architecture

The data flow, end to end

The hard part: reconstructing a decision months later

A review request can arrive weeks or months after the decision. By then models have been retrained and data has changed. The team made the decision record immutable and complete at the moment of decision, and linked each application event to the processing that handled it with distributed tracing. OpenTelemetry instrumentation for Kafka links the receive and process steps of a message in one trace, so analysts can follow an application from arrival to outcome6.

An explanation you generate later is a story. An explanation recorded at decision time is evidence. Build for the second.

Reason codes were generated from the model's own attributions and mapped to plain-language statements reviewed by legal and customer teams, so explanations were truthful without revealing model internals. More on evidence and evaluation in evaluation sets that predict production and high-impact AI in hiring.

How it ran

Key decisions and trade-offs

DecisionAlternativeWhy
One decision serviceScoring spread across servicesOne place to record, explain and govern
Record at decision timeReconstruct from logs on requestModels and data change; records must not
Reason codes from model attributionsGeneric decline messagesTruthful, useful and consistent explanations
Policy rules before modelsModel-only decisionsHard limits are easy to explain and audit
Prepare for the AI bill nowWait for the final textThe LGPD already requires most of this

What I'd do again, and differently

Again: consolidate decisions into one service before adding explanations; scattered logic cannot be explained. Differently: track overturned decisions from day one. They were the clearest signal of where models or rules needed work. Related: structured outputs and where I work.

item.title: Raising the cost of a fake face: deepfake-resistant customer onboarding for a Saudi digital bank
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: How a Saudi digital bank can harden remote onboarding against deepfakes: device attestation, liveness, layered risk signals, PDPL-aware data handling and human review.
item.content:encoded:
A Saudi digital bank onboarded customers entirely through its app, using a selfie video matched to an ID document. Deepfake tools were making that check cheaper to beat. The goal was to raise the cost of a fake identity well above the cost of the defences, without making genuine customers suffer.

The situation

A digital bank in Saudi Arabia opened accounts entirely in its app: the customer photographed their ID, recorded a short selfie video, and a vendor's model compared the two. It worked well for genuine customers. Fraud teams were seeing more attempts that looked like synthetic faces and replayed or injected video, and the existing check had one weak point: if the video was convincing, the account opened.

Why now. On 15 October 2026, SDAIA and the Communications, Space and Technology Commission launched the "It's AI" campaign on the risks of deepfakes, including fraud and identity theft, as part of Saudi Arabia's Year of AI1. The CST's guidance lists countermeasures including labelling AI-generated content, detection tools and international provenance standards such as C2PA2. For a bank whose front door is a camera, the message was clear: assume faces and voices can be faked.

What had to be true

  • No single check decides: several independent signals combine into a risk score.
  • Trust the capture, not just the content: prove video came from a genuine camera on a genuine device.
  • Genuine customers barely notice; friction rises only with risk.
  • Personal and biometric data handled under the PDPL, processed in the Kingdom and kept briefly34.
  • People in the loop for the hard cases, with good tools and guidance.

Architecture

The data flow, end to end

The hard part: attacks that never touch the camera

The most dangerous attacks skip the camera altogether, feeding generated or replayed video into a tampered app or emulator. Better face models do not help if the input is fake. The answer was to raise the attacker's cost at the capture step: device and app attestation, plus camera integrity checks, so injected video fails before any face comparison runs. The same reasoning appears in security design elsewhere: in the Model Context Protocol's analysis of client impersonation, adding attestation moves an attack from cheap to costly6.

Do not try to out-detect every deepfake. Make faking the capture expensive, and combine enough independent signals that no single fake is enough.

Where documents or media carried content credentials, the platform recorded them as one more signal; provenance standards such as C2PA are designed to show how content was created and edited5. Their absence was never treated as proof of fraud. Related reading: defender-first AI and patch cycles and detecting fraud rings with a knowledge graph.

How it ran

Key decisions and trade-offs

DecisionAlternativeWhy
Secure the capture step firstBuy a better deepfake detectorInjected video bypasses any detector downstream
Combine independent signalsOne strong biometric checkAn attacker must defeat several things at once
Risk-based step-upExtra checks for everyoneGenuine customers keep a fast journey
Human review for high riskAutomatic rejectionFewer false rejections, better fraud learning
In-Kingdom processing, short retentionVendor processing abroadSimpler under PDPL transfer rules and less to lose

What I'd do again, and differently

Again: red-team the onboarding flow before buying anything; it showed the weak point was capture, not matching. Differently: build reviewer tooling earlier. The quality of human decisions on hard cases depended more on the tools than on the guidance. See also Saudi PDPL and cross-border AI.

item.title: High-impact by design: running AI candidate screening under South Korea's AI Basic Act
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: How a Korean recruitment platform can run AI screening under the AI Basic Act: transparency, risk management, human oversight and evidence for every AI-assisted step.
item.content:encoded:
A South Korean recruitment platform used AI to match candidates to roles and summarise applications for employers. Under the AI Basic Act, AI used in hiring sits in the high-impact category. The goal was to keep the efficiency while making every AI-assisted step transparent, overseen by people and evidenced.

The situation

A South Korean recruitment platform served employers and job seekers. It used machine learning to match candidates to roles and, more recently, a language model to summarise applications and draft screening notes for recruiters. Employers liked the speed. Nobody had written down which steps used AI, how they were tested, or what a candidate could do if they disagreed.

Why now. South Korea's AI Basic Act took effect on 22 January 202612. Commentary describes core transparency duties for generative and high-impact AI, with high-impact uses, including areas such as hiring, bringing duties around risk management and human oversight23. Observers note the Act tries to balance innovation with social risk, and that its details are being filled in through implementing rules4. With enforcement maturing and enterprise customers asking for assurances, the platform chose to build for the high-impact obligations now.

What had to be true

  • Every AI use known and classified, with hiring uses treated as high-impact.
  • Candidates informed when AI is involved, with a route to human review.
  • A person decides: AI can rank and summarise, but no rejection without a recruiter's decision.
  • Models tested before release, including for differences across groups of candidates.
  • Evidence on demand for any application: inputs, outputs, model version and decision.

Architecture

The data flow, end to end

The hard part: evidence without slowing recruiters down

Oversight fails when it becomes paperwork. The platform made evidence a by-product of normal work: every AI call was traced with OpenTelemetry's GenAI conventions, capturing the input, the output, the tools used and the model, so any application could be reconstructed later5. The reviewer workbench put the AI summary next to the original CV with citations, so checking it took seconds rather than minutes.

In high-impact AI, the log is part of the product. If you cannot reconstruct a decision, you cannot defend it, improve it or explain it to the person it affected.

Personal data in traces was minimised and access-controlled; summaries were stored with the application, not in a separate analytics copy. Evaluation followed the approach in evaluation sets that predict production, with checks for differences across candidate groups added to the release gate. See also LLM observability with OpenTelemetry.

How it ran

Key decisions and trade-offs

DecisionAlternativeWhy
Treat all hiring AI as high-impactArgue each use out of scopeSimpler, defensible, and what employers expected
No automated rejectionsAuto-reject below a scoreKeeps a person accountable for adverse decisions
Summaries must cite the CVFree-text summariesReviewers can verify every claim quickly
Tracing as the evidence storeSeparate compliance loggingOne record for debugging, evaluation and accountability
Group-level checks in the release gatePeriodic audits onlyProblems found before candidates are affected

What I'd do again, and differently

Again: build the inventory and tracing first; everything else depended on them. Differently: design the candidate-facing review process earlier. Explaining an AI-assisted outcome in plain language was harder than producing the technical evidence. For broader governance context, see an AI governance programme across jurisdictions and ISO 42001 vs NIST AI RMF.

item.title: Ready before it is law: preparing a UK managed service provider for the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: How a UK managed service provider can prepare for regulation under the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill: privileged access, incident reporting and customer notice.
item.content:encoded:
A mid-sized UK managed service provider held administrator access to hundreds of customer environments. The Cyber Security and Resilience Bill would bring providers like it under the NIS regulations for the first time. The goal was to get ahead of it: control privileged access centrally, detect and report incidents quickly, and tell affected customers promptly.

The situation

A UK managed service provider looked after IT for several hundred organisations: small businesses, schools, professional services firms and a few public-sector suppliers. Its technicians held administrator access to customer networks, cloud tenants and line-of-business systems. Over the years, access had accumulated in shared accounts, remote management tools and scripts with stored credentials.

Why now. The Cyber Security and Resilience Bill would bring medium and large managed service providers within the scope of the NIS regulations, because of the privileged access they hold to customer systems12. It also proposes duties to report significant incidents and to identify and notify customers likely to be affected3. In October 2026 the Bill was still before Parliament4, but the direction was clear, and customers were already asking about it in renewals.

What had to be true

  • No standing administrator access to customer environments.
  • Every privileged session attributable to a named technician, approved and recorded.
  • Incidents detected and escalated fast, with a process that can support early notification and a fuller report.
  • Affected customers identifiable within minutes, not days of spreadsheet work.
  • Automation under the same rules as people, including AI-assisted tools.

Architecture

The data flow, end to end

The hard part: one front door for hundreds of environments

Access was spread across per-customer accounts in dozens of tools, each with its own login and its own way of revoking access. The design moved to a single identity provider for all technician and automation access, with customers' systems trusting it for scoped, time-limited sessions. The same principle is spreading in AI tooling: the Model Context Protocol's Enterprise-Managed Authorization lets an organisation provision access to many servers through its identity provider, scoped to users' groups and roles, instead of authenticating to each one separately6.

An MSP's biggest risk is its own access. Make every privileged session temporary, attributable and recorded, and most of the regulatory work follows.

Automation got no exemption. Scripts and AI-assisted tools used scoped service identities through the same broker, with no stored administrator passwords. More on that in securing MCP servers and sandboxing AI agents.

How it ran

Controls were mapped to the NCSC Cyber Assessment Framework, which organises security into outcomes for managing risk, protecting against attack, detecting events and minimising impact5. That gave customers and, later, a regulator a recognised way to read the programme.

Key decisions and trade-offs

DecisionAlternativeWhy
Prepare before the Bill passesWait for the final textThe core controls are good practice either way, and customers were asking now
Just-in-time access onlyStanding admin accounts with strong passwordsNo standing access means less to steal
One identity provider for people and automationPer-tool accountsCentral revocation and a single audit trail
Customer impact map as a systemSpreadsheetsPrompt notification needs answers in minutes
Map to the NCSC CAFA home-grown checklistA recognised framework customers and regulators understand

What I'd do again, and differently

Again: start with the privileged access inventory, because it surfaced most of the risk. Differently: run the first notification drill earlier. It showed that knowing which customers were affected was harder than detecting the incident. Related reading: defender-first AI and patch cycles and an AI copilot for the security operations centre.

item.title: Access by design: building an EU Data Act-ready data platform for a maker of connected equipment
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: How a European equipment maker can meet the EU Data Act's access-by-design rules: product data users can reach and share, consent, trade secrets and cloud portability.
item.content:encoded:
A European manufacturer of connected heating and ventilation equipment collected rich product data, but only its own service teams could use it. The EU Data Act turned that into an obligation: users must be able to access the data their products generate and share it with others. The goal was to build that into the product platform rather than bolt on a support process.

The situation

A manufacturer of connected heat pumps and ventilation units sold across the European Union. Its devices streamed temperatures, energy use, fault codes and runtime data to the cloud, where service teams used it for diagnostics and the product team used it to improve designs. Homeowners, installers and energy advisers saw only a slice of it in an app, and there was no way for a customer to take their data to someone else.

Why now. The EU Data Act gives users rights over the data their connected products and related services generate, including access and sharing with third parties they choose12. Its access-by-design obligation applies to connected products placed on the market after 12 September 2026, and commentators stress that it is an engineering obligation that has to be built into the product3. Separately, the Act's cloud switching rules prohibit switching charges from 12 January 20273. For a product line launching new models, both dates landed in the middle of the roadmap.

What had to be true

  • Users can get their data easily, in a usable format, without raising a support ticket.
  • Users can share it with an installer, energy adviser or app of their choice, and revoke that.
  • Personal data handled under the GDPR, because household energy patterns can identify people4.
  • Trade secrets protected through agreed measures, not used as a blanket excuse.
  • No cloud lock-in in the platform itself, in line with the switching rules.

Architecture

The data flow, end to end

The hard part: ingestion that scales with the fleet

Access by design starts at ingestion: if data is dropped, summarised too early or locked into a proprietary pipeline, users cannot get it later. The team standardised device telemetry on OTLP and placed a tier of OpenTelemetry Collectors in gateway mode behind a load balancer in each region, so data keeps flowing as the fleet grows and individual collectors can be replaced without loss5.

You cannot share data you never kept. Access by design is decided at ingestion, years before a user asks.

The second hard part was the line between raw data and know-how. Raw readings went into the user-accessible store; the predictive maintenance models and efficiency algorithms built from them stayed separate, with sharing partners bound by terms to protect anything sensitive. More on related patterns in OpenTelemetry Collector deployment patterns and data contracts.

How it ran

Key decisions and trade-offs

DecisionAlternativeWhy
Self-service access and sharingData requests through supportThe obligation is about design; support processes do not scale
Separate raw data from derived modelsOne store for everythingShare raw data freely while protecting know-how
Open telemetry protocol and formatsProprietary device protocolEasier access, portability and partner integration
A data catalogue users can readRaw field dumpsData is only useful if people know what it means
Infrastructure as code, open formatsDeep use of one cloud's proprietary servicesKeeps switching realistic as the rules intend

What I'd do again, and differently

Again: treat the catalogue as a product, because it made the data useful to customers and partners, not just compliant. Differently: settle the trade secret approach with legal before building the stores, since it shaped the data model more than any technical choice. Related reading: lakehouse catalogue strategy and the EU AI Act roadmap.

item.title: When the model is a material service provider: AI resilience for an Australian insurer under CPS 230
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: How an Australian insurer can treat AI model providers as material service providers under CPS 230: critical operations, tolerances, fallbacks and tested exit plans.
item.content:encoded:
An Australian general insurer had put AI into claims intake, customer service and fraud review, mostly through one hosted model provider. Nobody had asked what happens when that provider is slow, out of capacity or gone. Under APRA's CPS 230 that is a board-level question, and the goal was a credible answer.

The situation

A general insurer in Australia had moved quickly with AI. Claims intake used a hosted model to read documents and photos, the contact centre used it to draft responses, and the fraud team used it to summarise case files. Almost all of it ran through one external model provider, wired directly into each application.

CPS 230, APRA's prudential standard on operational risk management, has applied to banks, insurers and superannuation entities since 1 July 2025, with existing service provider contracts brought in at renewal or by 1 July 20261. It expects entities to identify critical operations, set tolerance levels for disruption, and manage material service providers2. The board asked a fair question: if the model provider has an outage, runs out of capacity or changes terms, what happens to claims?

Why now. Capacity is not a theoretical risk. Reporting on Microsoft's latest results notes that demand for its cloud still exceeds supply4, and AI capacity is the tightest part of that market. See the tech news update for 29 October.

What had to be true

  • AI dependencies visible in the same register as other material service providers.
  • Tolerance levels for each AI-assisted critical operation: how long, how degraded, before customers are harmed.
  • A tested alternative for every critical use, not a slide.
  • Privacy obligations met on every path, including fallbacks.
  • No rebuild of the applications: changes behind a common interface.

Architecture

The data flow, end to end

The hard part: deciding what to drop when capacity is short

Not every AI use is equally important, and pretending otherwise means everything fails together. The team tagged each request with the criticality of the operation it served, so the gateway could protect claims intake and shed or delay lower-priority work. The same idea appears in the Kubernetes Gateway API inference extension, where scheduling considers whether a request is critical and whether there is capacity before choosing a model server, and can drop non-critical requests when there is not5.

Resilience for AI is mostly a prioritisation decision. Decide in advance which work gets the last available capacity.

Every fallback path also had to meet privacy obligations. The OAIC's guidance on commercially available AI products expects due diligence on each product and ongoing review, not a one-off check3, so the second provider and the private model went through the same assessment as the primary. Routing patterns are covered in LLM model routing and Kubernetes inference gateways.

How it ran

Key decisions and trade-offs

DecisionAlternativeWhy
A single model gatewayProvider SDKs in each applicationFailover and exit become configuration, not rewrites
Second provider from a different vendorSecond region with the same vendorReduces concentration on one company's terms and capacity
Small private model as a floorHosted providers onlyA guaranteed baseline for the most critical step
Criticality tags on every requestTreat all AI traffic the sameProtects claims when capacity is short
Rehearse exit with live trafficA written exit planOnly tested plans count

What I'd do again, and differently

Again: put a gateway in front of every model call before adding a second provider; it made everything else cheap. Differently: build the evaluation set for each critical operation first. The slowest part of adding a provider was proving its answers were good enough, not wiring it in. See evaluation sets that predict production and AI incident postmortems.
